records.source: וַיַּגֵּ֤ד אַחְאָב֙ לְאִיזֶ֔בֶל אֵ֛ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה אֵלִיָּ֑הוּ וְאֵ֨ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָרַ֛ג אֶת־כָּל־הַנְּבִיאִ֖ים בֶּחָֽרֶב׃
records.gloss: And told Ahab to Jezebel all that had done Elijah, and all how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
pieces: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, including how he had put all the prophets to the sword.

L.1: And Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and all how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.

R.1: Ahab told his wife Jezebel everything Elijah had done. He told her how Elijah had killed all the prophets of Baal with the sword.

decisions.choice: all the prophets: the prophets of Baal killed at the Kishon
decisions.reason: Elijah had the prophets of Baal seized after the contest on Mount Carmel and killed them at the brook Kishon (18:40). They were Jezebel's own prophets, fed at her table (18:19), which is why the news provokes her.

decisions.choice: Jezebel: Ahab's wife, a princess of Sidon
decisions.reason: Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and brought the worship of Baal into Israel with her (16:31). She had already been killing the LORD's prophets (18:4, 13).

decisions.choice: his wife Jezebel; the prophets of Baal
decisions.reason: Readable reminds the reader who Jezebel was and which prophets were killed, as 16:31 and 18:40 tell.

records.heading: Elijah flees to Horeb

records.source: וַתִּשְׁלַ֤ח אִיזֶ֨בֶל֙ מַלְאָ֔ךְ אֶל־אֵלִיָּ֖הוּ לֵאמֹ֑ר כֹּֽה־יַעֲשׂ֤וּן אֱלֹהִים֙ וְכֹ֣ה יוֹסִפ֔וּן כִּֽי־כָעֵ֤ת מָחָר֙ אָשִׂ֣ים אֶֽת־נַפְשְׁךָ֔ כְּנֶ֖פֶשׁ אַחַ֥ד מֵהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And sent Jezebel a messenger to Elijah, saying, Thus may do [the] gods and thus may they add, for about [this] time tomorrow I will make your life like [the] life of one of them.
pieces: So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah to say, "May the gods deal with me ever so severely if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them."

L.2: And Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, "Thus may the gods do, and thus may they add, for about [this] time tomorrow I will make your life like the life of one of them."

R.2: So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah with this message: "May the gods punish me terribly if by this time tomorrow I have not killed you, just as you killed those prophets!"

decisions.choice: thus may the gods do, and thus may they add: a self-curse
decisions.reason: This is the oath form used in 1 Samuel 3:17, 14:44, 20:13 and 25:22: the speaker calls punishment, and more, down on herself if she does not keep her word. The punishment is left unnamed. Here the verbs are plural, so Jezebel swears by "the gods", her own gods, not by the God of Israel.

decisions.choice: for by this time tomorrow I will make your life like theirs: what the oath binds her to
decisions.reason: After an oath the word "for" introduces what the speaker swears to do. Jezebel vows to kill Elijah within a day, as he killed her prophets (verse 1).

decisions.choice: a messenger: the same word as "angel" in verses 5 and 7
decisions.reason: The word means one who is sent with a message. Jezebel's messenger brings a threat of death; the LORD's messenger will bring Elijah food and life (verses 5-7).

decisions.choice: the Hebrew text has the threat only
alternatives: the Greek translation begins the message with "If you are Elijah, I am Jezebel"
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation adds a line at the start of Jezebel's message setting her name against his. The Hebrew text, which is followed here, does not have it.

decisions.choice: May the gods deal with me ever so severely if ...; May the gods punish me terribly if ...
decisions.reason: The oath is worded as in 1 Samuel 3:17, 14:44, 20:13 and 25:22, with "me" supplied because the oath is a curse on the speaker. "If ... I have not" states plainly what the oath binds her to.

decisions.choice: I have not killed you, just as you killed those prophets
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what "make your life like the life of one of them" means.

records.source: וַיַּ֗רְא וַיָּ֨קָם֙ וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ אֶל־נַפְשׁ֔וֹ וַיָּבֹ֕א בְּאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֖בַע אֲשֶׁ֣ר לִֽיהוּדָ֑ה וַיַּנַּ֥ח אֶֽת־נַעֲר֖וֹ שָֽׁם׃
records.gloss: And he saw, and he arose and went for his life, and he came [to] Beersheba, which [belongs] to Judah, and he left his young man there.
pieces: When Elijah saw how things stood, he got up and fled for his life. He reached Beersheba, in Judah, and left his servant there.

L.3: And he saw [it], and he arose and went for his life, and he came to Beersheba, which [belongs] to Judah, and he left his young man there.

R.3: When Elijah saw what was happening, he got up and ran to save his life. He went to Beersheba, a town in Judah, far to the south, and left his servant there.

decisions.choice: he saw, as the vowels of the Hebrew text read
alternatives: he was afraid (the same consonants with different vowels, as some Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient translations read)
decisions.reason: The written consonants can be read as "he saw" or "he was afraid". The standard Hebrew text points them as "he saw", which is followed here: Elijah sees his danger. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek, Syriac and Latin translations read "he was afraid". Either way he runs for his life.

decisions.choice: went for his life: fled to save himself
decisions.reason: To go "for one's life" (2 Kings 7:7) is to flee to stay alive.

decisions.choice: Beersheba, which belongs to Judah: outside Ahab's kingdom
decisions.reason: Beersheba lay at the far south of the land ("from Dan to Beersheba", 1 Samuel 3:20). Belonging to Judah, it was in the southern kingdom, out of reach of Ahab and Jezebel, who ruled Israel in the north.

decisions.choice: his young man: his servant or attendant
decisions.reason: The word means a young man and is often used of a personal attendant (Genesis 22:3; Judges 7:10). Elijah goes on alone.

decisions.choice: Elijah saw how things stood; saw what was happening
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "he saw" with no object. Balanced and Readable supply what he saw: the danger Jezebel's message showed him.

decisions.choice: a town in Judah, far to the south
decisions.reason: Readable adds where Beersheba lay so the reader can see how far Elijah fled.

records.source: וְהֽוּא־הָלַ֤ךְ בַּמִּדְבָּר֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ י֔וֹם וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיֵּ֕שֶׁב תַּ֖חַת רֹ֣תֶם אֶחָ֑ד וַיִּשְׁאַ֤ל אֶת־נַפְשׁוֹ֙ לָמ֔וּת וַיֹּ֣אמֶר׀רַ֗ב עַתָּ֤ה יְהוָה֙ קַ֣ח נַפְשִׁ֔י כִּֽי־לֹא־ט֥וֹב אָנֹכִ֖י מֵאֲבֹתָֽי׃
records.gloss: And he went in the wilderness a journey of a day, and came and sat under a broom tree, one, and he asked his life to die, and said, Enough! Now, Yahweh, take my life, for not good [am] I more than my fathers.
pieces: But he himself went on a day's journey into the wilderness. He came to a broom tree and sat down under it, and he prayed that he might die. "It is enough," he said. "Now, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, take my life, for I am no better than my {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}."

L.4: And he himself went into the wilderness a day's journey, and he came and sat under a certain broom tree; and he asked for himself that he might die, and said, "[It is] enough! Now, O {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, take my life, for I [am] not better than my fathers."

R.4: Then Elijah walked on alone into the desert for a whole day. He sat down under a broom bush and asked to die. "I have had enough, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}," he said. "Take my life now. I am no better than my {{gender:ancestors|fathers}}."

decisions.choice: broom tree: a desert shrub
decisions.reason: The broom is a bush of the southern wilderness that can grow to the height of a small tree and gives a little shade. Its roots were burned for charcoal (Psalm 120:4; Job 30:4).

decisions.choice: asked his life to die: asked that he might die
decisions.reason: The same words are used of Jonah's wish to die (Jonah 4:8).

decisions.choice: for I am not better than my fathers: why he wants to die
alternatives: for I am no better than my ancestors, who also failed
for I am no better than my ancestors, who all died
decisions.reason: Elijah may mean that he has done no better than those before him at turning Israel back to the LORD, or simply that he is mortal like them and is ready to go the same way. The words do not say which.

decisions.choice: take my life: echoes Moses' prayer
decisions.reason: Moses too, worn out by the people, asked the LORD to kill him (Numbers 11:15). Elijah's journey to Horeb (verse 8) will make the likeness to Moses clearer.

decisions.choice: LORD, without the article
decisions.reason: When the name is used to call on God directly, English writes "LORD" without "the".

decisions.choice: desert; broom bush
decisions.reason: Readable uses everyday words for the wilderness and for the low tree.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁכַּב֙ וַיִּישַׁ֔ן תַּ֖חַת רֹ֣תֶם אֶחָ֑ד וְהִנֵּֽה־זֶ֤ה מַלְאָךְ֙ נֹגֵ֣עַ בּ֔וֹ וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹ ק֥וּם אֱכֽוֹל׃
records.gloss: And he lay down and slept under a broom tree, one, and look! this, an angel touching him, and he said to him, Arise, eat.
pieces: Then he lay down and slept under the broom tree. And all at once an angel touched him and said to him, "Get up and eat."

L.5: And he lay down and slept under a certain broom tree; and look, an angel [was] touching him, and he said to him, "Arise, eat."

R.5: Then he lay down under the bush and went to sleep. All at once an angel touched him. "Get up and eat!" the angel said.

decisions.choice: an angel: a messenger from God
decisions.reason: The word is the same as Jezebel's "messenger" in verse 2. Verse 7 says who sent this one: he is "the angel of the LORD".

decisions.choice: look, an angel touching him: a sudden surprise
decisions.reason: The word "look" with the participle shows the scene through Elijah's eyes as he wakes.

decisions.choice: the broom tree
decisions.reason: The tree was introduced in verse 4; Balanced points back to it.

records.source: וַיַּבֵּ֕ט וְהִנֵּ֧ה מְרַאֲשֹׁתָ֛יו עֻגַ֥ת רְצָפִ֖ים וְצַפַּ֣חַת מָ֑יִם וַיֹּ֣אכַל וַיֵּ֔שְׁתְּ וַיָּ֖שָׁב וַיִּשְׁכָּֽב׃
records.gloss: And he looked, and look! at his head [was] a cake of hot stones and a jar of water; and he ate and drank, and he returned and lay down.
pieces: He looked, and there by his head was a loaf baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and then lay down again.

L.6: And he looked, and look, at his head [was] a cake [baked on] hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank, and lay down again.

R.6: He looked around. Next to his head was some bread baked on hot stones, and a jar of water. So he ate and drank, and then he lay down again.

decisions.choice: a cake of hot stones: a round flat loaf baked on heated stones
decisions.reason: Bread was often baked by laying the dough on stones heated in the fire (compare Genesis 18:6). The loaf here seems to have been made ready for Elijah while he slept.

decisions.choice: a jar: a small pottery water jug
decisions.reason: The same word is used for the water jar David took from beside the sleeping Saul's head (1 Samuel 26:11-12).

decisions.choice: he returned and lay down: he lay down again
decisions.reason: The verb "return" before another verb often means doing it again.

decisions.choice: [baked on]
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says simply "a cake of hot stones"; Literal brackets the words that show what the phrase means.

records.source: וַיָּשָׁב֩ מַלְאַ֨ךְ יְהוָ֤ה׀שֵׁנִית֙ וַיִּגַּע־בּ֔וֹ וַיֹּ֖אמֶר ק֣וּם אֱכֹ֑ל כִּ֛י רַ֥ב מִמְּךָ֖ הַדָּֽרֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And returned [the] angel of Yahweh a second [time] and touched him, and said, Arise, eat, for too great for you [is] the journey.
pieces: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came back a second time, touched him and said, "Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you."

L.7: And the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came back a second time and touched him and said, "Arise, eat, for the journey [is] too great for you."

R.7: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came back a second time. He touched Elijah and said, "Get up and eat! The trip ahead of you is too long for you."

decisions.choice: the angel of Yahweh: the messenger the LORD has sent
decisions.reason: The narrator now names the angel of verse 5 as the LORD's own messenger (see Judges 2:1; 6:11). The LORD answers Elijah's prayer to die not with death but with food and strength.

decisions.choice: for the journey is too great for you: the journey still ahead
decisions.reason: Elijah has not said he is going anywhere; the angel speaks of a journey still to come, the one to Horeb (verse 8).

decisions.choice: the trip ahead of you
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the journey is still to come.

records.source: וַיָּ֖קָם וַיֹּ֣אכַל וַיִּשְׁתֶּ֑ה וַיֵּ֜לֶךְ בְּכֹ֣חַ׀הָאֲכִילָ֣ה הַהִ֗יא אַרְבָּעִ֥ים יוֹם֙ וְאַרְבָּעִ֣ים לַ֔יְלָה עַ֛ד הַ֥ר הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים חֹרֵֽב׃
records.gloss: And he arose and ate and drank, and went in [the] strength of the food, that, forty day[s] and forty night[s] to [the] mountain of God, Horeb.
pieces: So he got up, ate and drank, and in the strength of that food he walked forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God.

L.8: And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to the mountain of God, Horeb.

R.8: So Elijah got up and ate and drank. That food gave him strength to walk for forty days and forty nights. He walked all the way to Horeb, the mountain of God.

decisions.choice: forty days and forty nights: as Moses on the mountain
decisions.reason: Moses was on the mountain with the LORD forty days and forty nights (Exodus 24:18), and the second time he neither ate nor drank (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9, 18). Elijah, kept alive by the food God gave, makes his own forty days' journey to the same mountain.

decisions.choice: Horeb, the mountain of God: the mountain also called Sinai
decisions.reason: Horeb is the name Deuteronomy and Exodus 3:1 use for the mountain where the LORD met Moses and gave the covenant (Exodus 3:1; Deuteronomy 5:2). Elijah, the defender of that covenant (verse 10), goes back to where it began.

decisions.choice: forty days: a long journey, more than the distance needs
decisions.reason: From Beersheba to the traditional site of Sinai is about two weeks' walk. The forty days may include wandering, or the number may be chosen to match Moses' forty days; the text gives no route.

decisions.choice: to Horeb, the mountain of God
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the name first, as English usually does.

records.source: וַיָּבֹא־שָׁ֥ם אֶל־הַמְּעָרָ֖ה וַיָּ֣לֶן שָׁ֑ם וְהִנֵּ֤ה דְבַר־יְהוָה֙ אֵלָ֔יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ מַה־לְּךָ֥ פֹ֖ה אֵלִיָּֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And he came there to the cave and spent the night there; and look! [the] word of Yahweh [was] to him, and he said to him, What to you here, Elijah?
pieces: There he came to the cave and spent the night in it. Then the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to him: "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

L.9: And he came there to the cave and spent the night there. And look, the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [came] to him, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to him, "What [is it] to you here, Elijah?"

R.9: When he got there, he went into a cave and spent the night. Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} spoke to him. He asked, "Elijah, what are you doing here?"

decisions.choice: the cave: a particular cave on the mountain
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "the cave", as if it were a place already known. It may recall the cleft in the rock where the LORD put Moses as his glory passed by (Exodus 33:21-22), though a different word is used there.

decisions.choice: what to you here: what are you doing here?
decisions.reason: The question asks what has brought Elijah here and what he wants. It is asked again, in the same words, in verse 13.

decisions.choice: the word of Yahweh came to him: the LORD spoke to him
decisions.reason: This is the usual way of saying that the LORD gave a prophet a message (17:2, 8; 18:1).

decisions.choice: the LORD spoke to him. He asked
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that it was the LORD who spoke, and gives his words as a question he asked.

decisions.choice: What are you doing here
decisions.reason: The Hebrew idiom "what to you here?" is given as the natural question.

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ קַנֹּ֨א קִנֵּ֜אתִי לַיהוָ֣ה׀אֱלֹהֵ֣י צְבָא֗וֹת כִּֽי־עָזְב֤וּ בְרִֽיתְךָ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתֶ֣יךָ הָרָ֔סוּ וְאֶת־נְבִיאֶ֖יךָ הָרְג֣וּ בֶחָ֑רֶב וָֽאִוָּתֵ֤ר אֲנִי֙ לְבַדִּ֔י וַיְבַקְשׁ֥וּ אֶת־נַפְשִׁ֖י לְקַחְתָּֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And he said, Being zealous I have been zealous for Yahweh God of hosts, for have forsaken your covenant [the] sons of Israel; your altars they have torn down, and your prophets they have killed with the sword; and am left I, I alone, and they seek my life to take it.
pieces: He answered, "I have been very zealous for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies, because the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} have abandoned {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} covenant. They have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars and put {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets to the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life."

L.10: And he said, "I have been very zealous for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of hosts, for the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel have forsaken {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} covenant; they have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars, and they have killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets with the sword. And I am left, I alone, and they seek my life, to take it."

R.10: Elijah answered, "I have worked with all my heart for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies. But the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} have turned away from {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} covenant. They have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars and killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets with swords. I am the only one left, and now they want to kill me too."

decisions.choice: being zealous I have been zealous: I have been jealous for the LORD's honor with all my strength
decisions.reason: The verb is used of the LORD's own jealousy for his people's loyalty (Exodus 20:5; 34:14), and of Phinehas, who acted against Israel's worship of the Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:11, 13). Repeating the verb makes it strong. Elijah means he has fought for the LORD alone against the worship of Baal.

decisions.choice: Yahweh God of hosts: the LORD who commands the armies of heaven and earth
decisions.reason: "Hosts" means armies. The title names the LORD as ruler over every power (1 Samuel 1:3; 17:45).

decisions.choice: I am left, I alone: Elijah's own view
decisions.reason: Elijah knows of the hundred prophets Obadiah hid (18:4, 13), so he may mean he is the only one still standing openly for the LORD. The LORD answers his words in verse 18.

decisions.choice: forsaken your covenant: the covenant made at Horeb
decisions.reason: Elijah speaks at the mountain where the covenant was given (verse 8; Deuteronomy 5:2). Tearing down the LORD's altars and killing his prophets (18:4, 30) are the signs that Israel has broken it.

decisions.choice: very zealous; worked with all my heart
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep "zealous" so the link with Phinehas (Numbers 25:11) can be seen; the repeated verb becomes "very". Readable says what the zeal was.

decisions.choice: God of Armies
decisions.reason: As in the other books of Kings and Samuel, Balanced and Readable say "Armies" for "hosts".

records.source: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר צֵ֣א וְעָמַדְתָּ֣ בָהָר֮ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָה֒ וְהִנֵּ֧ה יְהוָ֣ה עֹבֵ֗ר וְר֣וּחַ גְּדוֹלָ֡ה וְחָזָ֞ק מְפָרֵק֩ הָרִ֨ים וּמְשַׁבֵּ֤ר סְלָעִים֙ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה לֹ֥א בָר֖וּחַ יְהוָ֑ה וְאַחַ֤ר הָר֨וּחַרַ֔עַשׁ לֹ֥א בָרַ֖עַשׁ יְהוָֽה׃
records.gloss: And he said, Go out and stand on the mountain before Yahweh; and look! Yahweh [was] passing by, and a wind great and strong [was] tearing mountains and breaking rocks before Yahweh; not in the wind [was] Yahweh; and after the wind an earthquake; not in the earthquake [was] Yahweh.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Go out and stand on the mountain in the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And there, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was passing by. A mighty, fierce wind was splitting the mountains and smashing the rocks to pieces ahead of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, but {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake; {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was not in the earthquake.

L.11: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Go out and stand on the mountain before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And look, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [was] passing by, and a wind, great and strong, [was] tearing [the] mountains and breaking [the] rocks in pieces before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [was] not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake; {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [was] not in the earthquake.

R.11: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Go out and stand on the mountain in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} passed by. A very strong wind blew. It split the mountains apart and broke the rocks into pieces in front of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was not in the wind. Next the ground shook in an earthquake. But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was not in the earthquake.

decisions.choice: look, Yahweh was passing by: the narrator tells what happened
alternatives: for look, Yahweh is about to pass by: still part of the LORD's words to Elijah
decisions.reason: The Hebrew does not mark where the LORD's words end. The participle "passing by" can describe what was happening or what was about to happen. Here the LORD's command is taken to end with "before Yahweh", and the rest is the narrator's account. Elijah does not actually go out until verse 13, so he seems to have stayed in the cave while the wind, earthquake and fire passed.

decisions.choice: Yahweh passing by: as the LORD passed by Moses on this mountain
decisions.reason: On the same mountain the LORD made his goodness "pass by" Moses, who was hidden in a cleft of the rock, and proclaimed his name (Exodus 33:19-22; 34:6). Elijah in his cave stands where Moses stood.

decisions.choice: wind and earthquake: signs of God's coming, but the LORD was not in them
decisions.reason: When the LORD came down on Sinai, the mountain shook and there was fire and storm (Exodus 19:16-18; compare Judges 5:4-5; Psalm 18:8-16). Here those signs come, but the narrator says each time that the LORD was not in them. He does not say that God has stopped using such powers: he sent fire on Carmel only days before (18:38).

decisions.choice: a wind: moving air, a storm wind
decisions.reason: The word can also mean "breath" or "spirit", but beside the earthquake and fire it is a storm that splits rocks.

decisions.choice: A mighty, fierce wind was splitting ... and smashing
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the strength of the wind and the force of its work in plain, vivid words.

decisions.choice: The LORD said
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "he said"; the speaker is the LORD, whose word came to Elijah in verse 9.

records.source: וְאַחַ֤ר הָרַ֨עַשׁ֙ אֵ֔שׁ לֹ֥א בָאֵ֖שׁ יְהוָ֑ה וְאַחַ֣ר הָאֵ֔שׁ ק֖וֹל דְּמָמָ֥ה דַקָּֽה׃
records.gloss: And after the earthquake a fire; not in the fire [was] Yahweh; and after the fire a sound of silence thin.
pieces: Then came fire after the earthquake, but {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was not in the fire. And when the fire had passed, a faint sound, thin as silence.

L.12: And after the earthquake, a fire; {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [was] not in the fire. And after the fire, a sound of thin silence.

R.12: Next there was a fire. But {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} was not in the fire. When the fire was over, there was a very soft sound, almost like silence.

decisions.choice: a sound of thin silence: a sound so faint it is almost silence
alternatives: a still small voice (an older rendering)
decisions.reason: The first word means "sound" or "voice". The second means stillness or silence: the calm after a storm (Psalm 107:29), or the hush before a voice is heard (Job 4:16). The third means thin, fine, or crushed small, like the fine flakes of manna (Exodus 16:14) or finely ground incense (Leviticus 16:12). Put together they make a deliberate puzzle: a sound that is hardly a sound. Some take it as a gentle whisper or a soft breath of air. The text does not say that the LORD was in this sound, but after it the voice speaks (verse 13).

decisions.choice: fire: the LORD was not in it either
decisions.reason: Fire was the sign of the LORD's presence at Sinai (Exodus 19:18) and the answer to Elijah's prayer on Carmel (18:38). Here, after wind, earthquake and fire, the LORD comes to Elijah in near silence.

decisions.choice: a faint sound, thin as silence; a very soft sound, almost like silence
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the paradox of the Hebrew, a sound that is close to silence, rather than settle it as a whisper or a breeze.

decisions.choice: a sound of thin silence, not "a still small voice"
decisions.reason: "A still small voice" is the King James Version's well-known wording. It keeps "small" for the third word but turns the silence into a voice, which the Hebrew does not say until verse 13. "A gentle whisper" makes it a sound of speech. Our wording keeps the stillness the Hebrew names.

records.source: וַיְהִ֣י׀כִּשְׁמֹ֣עַ אֵלִיָּ֗הוּ וַיָּ֤לֶט פָּנָיו֙ בְּאַדַּרְתּ֔וֹ וַיֵּצֵ֕א וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֖ד פֶּ֣תַח הַמְּעָרָ֑ה וְהִנֵּ֤ה אֵלָיו֙ ק֔וֹל וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מַה־לְּךָ֥ פֹ֖ה אֵלִיָּֽהוּ׃
records.gloss: And it was, when heard Elijah, and he wrapped his face in his cloak, and went out and stood [at the] entrance of the cave; and look! to him a voice, and it said, What to you here, Elijah?
pieces: When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his cloak around his face, went out, and stood at the cave's mouth. Then a voice came to him: "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

L.13: And it happened, when Elijah heard [it], that he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. And look, a voice [came] to him and said, "What [is it] to you here, Elijah?"

R.13: When Elijah heard the sound, he covered his face with his cloak. He went out and stood at the opening of the cave. Then a voice said to him, "Elijah, what are you doing here?"

decisions.choice: he wrapped his face in his cloak: in awe of God's presence
decisions.reason: Moses hid his face at the burning bush because he was afraid to look at God (Exodus 3:6), and on this mountain no one could see the LORD's face and live (Exodus 33:20-23). Elijah covers his face because he knows the LORD is near.

decisions.choice: a voice: the same word as "sound" in verse 12
decisions.reason: The faint "sound" of verse 12 now becomes a "voice" that speaks. The word is the same.

decisions.choice: cloak: a prophet's outer garment
decisions.reason: The word names a wide outer robe. Elijah's cloak will be thrown over Elisha (verse 19) and later parts the Jordan (2 Kings 2:8, 13-14).

decisions.choice: What are you doing here, Elijah?: the question of verse 9 repeated
decisions.reason: The LORD asks the same question in the same words, after all Elijah has seen and heard.

decisions.choice: cloak
decisions.reason: "Cloak" is used rather than the older word "mantle", here and in verse 19.

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ קַנֹּ֨א קִנֵּ֜אתִי לַיהוָ֣ה׀אֱלֹהֵ֣י צְבָא֗וֹת כִּֽי־עָזְב֤וּ בְרִֽיתְךָ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֶת־מִזְבְּחֹתֶ֣יךָ הָרָ֔סוּ וְאֶת־נְבִיאֶ֖יךָ הָרְג֣וּ בֶחָ֑רֶב וָאִוָּתֵ֤ר אֲנִי֙ לְבַדִּ֔י וַיְבַקְשׁ֥וּ אֶת־נַפְשִׁ֖י לְקַחְתָּֽהּ׃ס
records.gloss: And he said, Being zealous I have been zealous for Yahweh God of hosts, for have forsaken your covenant [the] sons of Israel; your altars they have torn down, and your prophets they have killed with the sword; and am left I, I alone, and they seek my life to take it.
pieces: He answered, "I have been very zealous for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies, because the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} have abandoned {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} covenant. They have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars and put {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets to the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life."

L.14: And he said, "I have been very zealous for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of hosts, for the {{gender:children|sons}} of Israel have forsaken {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} covenant; they have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars, and they have killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets with the sword. And I am left, I alone, and they seek my life, to take it."

R.14: Elijah answered, "I have worked with all my heart for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies. But the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} have turned away from {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} covenant. They have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars and killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets with swords. I am the only one left, and now they want to kill me too."

decisions.choice: the same answer as verse 10, word for word
decisions.reason: Elijah repeats his complaint exactly as he gave it in verse 10. The wind, the earthquake, the fire and the quiet sound have not changed what he says. The LORD does not argue with him but gives him new work (verses 15-18). See verse 10 for the words themselves.

decisions.choice: worded exactly as verse 10
decisions.reason: Because the Hebrew repeats verse 10 exactly, every level repeats its wording from verse 10 so the reader sees the repetition.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֵלָ֔יו לֵ֛ךְ שׁ֥וּב לְדַרְכְּךָ֖ מִדְבַּ֣רָה דַמָּ֑שֶׂקוּבָ֗אתָ וּמָשַׁחְתָּ֧ אֶת־חֲזָאֵ֛ל לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־אֲרָֽם׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh to him, Go, return on your way [to the] wilderness of Damascus, and you will come and anoint Hazael as king over Aram.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Go back the way you came, and go to the wilderness of Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael as king over Aram.

L.15: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus; and you will come and anoint Hazael as king over Aram.

R.15: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said to him, "Go back the way you came, and go on to the desert near Damascus. When you get there, pour oil on Hazael's head to make him king of Aram.

decisions.choice: Hazael and Aram: the kingdom of the Arameans, whose capital was Damascus
decisions.reason: Aram lay north-east of Israel, with Damascus as its capital, and was often at war with Israel (20:1; 22:1-4). Hazael was an official of its king Ben-hadad (2 Kings 8:7-15).

decisions.choice: anoint: pour oil on someone to set them apart for an office
decisions.reason: Kings were anointed (1 Samuel 10:1; 16:13), and so were priests (Exodus 29:7). Only here is a prophet told to anoint another prophet (verse 16).

decisions.choice: the three anointings: how they were carried out
decisions.reason: Elijah himself does not anoint Hazael or Jehu. He calls Elisha by throwing his cloak over him (verse 19). Later Elisha tells Hazael that he will be king (2 Kings 8:13), and a young prophet sent by Elisha anoints Jehu (2 Kings 9:1-6). The LORD's commission is fulfilled through Elijah's successor.

decisions.choice: go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus: go back north, toward Damascus
decisions.reason: Elijah is to go back the way he came, and on past Israel to the wilderness near Damascus. The man who ran from Jezebel is sent back into danger with a task.

decisions.choice: pour oil on Hazael's head to make him king
decisions.reason: Readable explains what it means to anoint someone as king.

records.heading: The call of Elisha

records.source: וְאֵת֙ יֵה֣וּא בֶן־נִמְשִׁ֔י תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְמֶ֖לֶךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְאֶת־אֱלִישָׁ֤ע בֶּן־שָׁפָט֙ מֵאָבֵ֣ל מְחוֹלָ֔ה תִּמְשַׁ֥ח לְנָבִ֖יא תַּחְתֶּֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: And Jehu son of Nimshi you will anoint as king over Israel; and Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah you will anoint as prophet in your place.
pieces: Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel, and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to be prophet in your place.

L.16: And Jehu son of Nimshi you will anoint as king over Israel; and Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah you will anoint as prophet in your place.

R.16: Also anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king of Israel. And anoint Elisha son of Shaphat, from the town of Abel-meholah, to be the prophet who will take your place.

decisions.choice: Jehu son of Nimshi: a commander who would end Ahab's dynasty
decisions.reason: Jehu was a commander in Israel's army. He became king by overthrowing Ahab's son Joram and destroying Ahab's family and the worship of Baal (2 Kings 9-10). He is called "son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi" in 2 Kings 9:2, so "son" here means descendant.

decisions.choice: Abel-meholah: a town in the Jordan valley
decisions.reason: The town lay near the Jordan, south of the Sea of Galilee (Judges 7:22; 1 Kings 4:12).

decisions.choice: as prophet in your place: as your successor
decisions.reason: Elijah has said he is the only one left (verses 10, 14). The LORD names another to carry on his work after him.

decisions.choice: from the town of Abel-meholah
decisions.reason: Readable adds "the town of" so the reader knows this is a place name.

records.source: וְהָיָ֗ה הַנִּמְלָ֛ט מֵחֶ֥רֶב חֲזָאֵ֖ל יָמִ֣ית יֵה֑וּא וְהַנִּמְלָ֛ט מֵחֶ֥רֶב יֵה֖וּא יָמִ֥ית אֱלִישָֽׁע׃
records.gloss: And it will be, the [one] escaping from [the] sword of Hazael, will put to death Jehu; and the [one] escaping from [the] sword of Jehu, will put to death Elisha.
pieces: Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu will put to death, and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha will put to death.

L.17: And it will be [that] the one who escapes from the sword of Hazael, Jehu will put to death; and the one who escapes from the sword of Jehu, Elisha will put to death.

R.17: Jehu will kill anyone who escapes from Hazael's sword, and Elisha will kill anyone who escapes from Jehu's sword.

decisions.choice: the sword of Hazael and Jehu: the LORD's judgment on Israel's worship of Baal
decisions.reason: Hazael would make war on Israel and kill many (2 Kings 8:12; 10:32-33), and Jehu would kill Ahab's family and the worshipers of Baal (2 Kings 10:11, 18-28). The LORD answers Elijah's complaint that Israel has forsaken the covenant.

decisions.choice: Elisha will put to death: by the word the LORD gives him
alternatives: Elisha himself will carry out executions
decisions.reason: Elisha is never said to kill with a sword. His word brings death on those who mock the LORD (2 Kings 2:23-24), and he announces the deaths that Hazael and Jehu will bring (2 Kings 8:10-13; 9:1-10). The judgment comes through the prophet's word.

decisions.choice: the one who escapes: not in time order
decisions.reason: The three are named as a chain of judgment, not in the order things happened: Elisha's ministry begins first, and Jehu's revolt (2 Kings 9) came before most of Hazael's wars.

records.source: וְהִשְׁאַרְתִּ֥י בְיִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שִׁבְעַ֣ת אֲלָפִ֑ים כָּל־הַבִּרְכַּ֗יִם אֲשֶׁ֤ר לֹֽא־כָֽרְעוּ֙ לַבַּ֔עַל וְכָ֨ל־הַפֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־נָשַׁ֖ק לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And I will leave in Israel seven thousand, all the knees which not have bowed to Baal, and every mouth which not has kissed him.
pieces: Yet I will leave 7,000 in Israel, everyone whose knees have not bent to Baal and whose lips have not kissed him."

L.18: And I will leave in Israel 7,000, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him."

R.18: But I will keep 7,000 people in Israel alive. They have never knelt down to Baal or kissed his idol."

decisions.choice: I will leave: what the LORD will do
alternatives: I have kept: what the LORD has already done
decisions.reason: The verb form here normally speaks of the future, following on from verse 17: when judgment comes, the LORD will spare these. It can also be read as a statement that the LORD has already kept them for himself, and that is how Paul quotes the verse (Romans 11:4). Either way Elijah is not alone.

decisions.choice: bowing the knee and kissing: acts of worship
decisions.reason: Worshipers knelt before an idol and kissed it (Hosea 13:2). The 7,000 had kept away from both.

decisions.choice: 7,000: the faithful remnant
decisions.reason: This answers Elijah's "I am left, I alone" (verses 10, 14). The number is large and complete, and the LORD, not Elijah, knows who they are.
Numbers above ninety-nine are written in figures at every level.

decisions.choice: kissed his idol
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that "kissing him" means kissing an image of Baal.

records.source: וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ מִ֠שָּׁם וַיִּמְצָ֞א אֶת־אֱלִישָׁ֤ע בֶּן־שָׁפָט֙ וְה֣וּא חֹרֵ֔שׁ שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֤ר צְמָדִים֙ לְפָנָ֔יו וְה֖וּא בִּשְׁנֵ֣ים הֶעָשָׂ֑ר וַיַּעֲבֹ֤ר אֵלִיָּ֨הוּ֙ אֵלָ֔יו וַיַּשְׁלֵ֥ךְ אַדַּרְתּ֖וֹ אֵלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And he went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat, and he [was] plowing, twelve yoke before him, and he with the twelfth; and passed Elijah to him and threw his cloak to him.
pieces: So Elijah went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing. There were twelve pairs of oxen ahead of him, and he was with the twelfth pair. Elijah went over to him and threw his cloak over him.

L.19: And he went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat, and he [was] plowing; twelve yoke [of oxen were] before him, and he [was] with the twelfth. And Elijah passed over to him and threw his cloak on him.

R.19: So Elijah left there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. Elisha was plowing a field with twelve pairs of oxen, one pair behind another, and he was driving the last pair. Elijah went up to him and threw his own cloak over him.

decisions.choice: twelve yoke of oxen: a large farm at work
decisions.reason: A yoke was a pair of oxen pulling one plow. Twelve teams plowing one behind another show that Elisha's family was well off. Elisha drove the last pair, behind the others.

decisions.choice: threw his cloak over him: a sign that Elisha was called
decisions.reason: The cloak was Elijah's mark as a prophet (2 Kings 1:8). Throwing it over Elisha claims him for Elijah's work, and Elisha understands at once (verse 20). When Elijah is taken up, Elisha takes up the same cloak (2 Kings 2:13-14).

decisions.choice: passed over to him: went across to him
decisions.reason: The verb with "to him" means Elijah crossed over to where Elisha was; it may also suggest that he went past as he threw the cloak, without stopping (verse 20).

decisions.choice: pairs of oxen; the twelfth pair
decisions.reason: "Yoke" means a pair of oxen yoked together; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: וַיַּעֲזֹ֣ב אֶת־הַבָּקָ֗ר וַיָּ֨רָץ֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י אֵֽלִיָּ֔הוּ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֶשְּׁקָה־נָּא֙ לְאָבִ֣י וּלְאִמִּ֔י וְאֵלְכָ֖ה אַחֲרֶ֑יךָ וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ לֵ֣ךְ שׁ֔וּב כִּ֥י מֶה־עָשִׂ֖יתִי לָֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And he left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, Let me kiss please my father and my mother, and I will go after you. And he said to him, Go, return, for what have I done to you?
pieces: Then Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah and said, "Let me kiss my father and my mother goodbye, please, and then I will follow you." Elijah said to him, "Go back. What have I done to you?"

L.20: And he left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, "Please let me kiss my father and my mother, and [then] I will go after you." And he said to him, "Go, return, for what have I done to you?"

R.20: Elisha left the oxen and ran after Elijah. "Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye," he said. "Then I will come with you." Elijah said to him, "Go back, then. What have I done to you?"

decisions.choice: Go, return, for what have I done to you?: Elisha is free to go home, but must weigh what the cloak meant
alternatives: Go back; I have done nothing to stop you
Go back if you like, but remember what I have just done to you
decisions.reason: The words are short and can be heard in more than one way. Elijah may be giving Elisha leave to go home, since he has laid no command on him. Or he may be reminding Elisha that the cloak was a real call that he must not take lightly. Elisha's answer in verse 21 shows that he took the call seriously.

decisions.choice: I will go after you: I will follow you as your disciple
decisions.reason: To "go after" someone means to follow them and become their follower (verse 21).

decisions.choice: let me kiss my father and my mother: a farewell
decisions.reason: Elisha asks to say goodbye to his family before leaving home for good.

decisions.choice: kiss ... goodbye
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "goodbye" to show that the kiss is a farewell.

decisions.choice: Elijah said
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "he said"; Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

records.source: וַיָּ֨שָׁב מֵאַחֲרָ֜יו וַיִּקַּ֣ח אֶת־צֶ֧מֶד הַבָּקָ֣ר וַיִּזְבָּחֵ֗הוּ וּבִכְלִ֤י הַבָּקָר֙ בִּשְּׁלָ֣ם הַבָּשָׂ֔ר וַיִּתֵּ֥ן לָעָ֖ם וַיֹּאכֵ֑לוּ וַיָּ֗קָם וַיֵּ֛לֶךְ אַחֲרֵ֥י אֵלִיָּ֖הוּ וַיְשָׁרְתֵֽהוּ׃פ
records.gloss: And he returned from after him and took the yoke of the oxen and sacrificed it, and with [the] equipment of the oxen he boiled them, the flesh, and gave to the people, and they ate. And he arose and went after Elijah and served him.
pieces: Elisha turned back from following him. He took the pair of oxen and slaughtered them, boiled their meat using the oxen's gear for fuel, and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah and became his attendant.

L.21: And he turned back from [following] him and took the yoke of oxen and slaughtered them, and with the oxen's equipment he boiled their flesh and gave [it] to the people, and they ate. And he arose and went after Elijah and served him.

R.21: So Elisha went back. He took his pair of oxen and killed them. He burned the wooden plow and yoke to cook the meat. Then he gave the meat to the people, and they ate it. After that he got up and went with Elijah, and became his helper.

decisions.choice: slaughtered them: killed them for a meal, perhaps as a sacrifice
decisions.reason: The verb is often used of killing animals as a sacrifice, but it can also mean killing them for a feast (1 Samuel 28:24). Here the meat is shared with the people, as at a fellowship sacrifice.

decisions.choice: with the oxen's equipment he boiled the flesh: he burned his plowing gear
decisions.reason: Elisha uses the wooden yoke and plow as fuel. By killing his oxen and burning his tools he gives up his old work and makes a clean break: there is no farm to go back to.

decisions.choice: served him: became his personal attendant
decisions.reason: The word is used of Joshua, Moses' assistant (Exodus 24:13; 33:11; Numbers 11:28). Like Joshua after Moses, Elisha will succeed his master.

decisions.choice: using the oxen's gear for fuel; burned the wooden plow and yoke
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say how the equipment was used: as firewood for cooking.

decisions.choice: became his attendant; became his helper
decisions.reason: The verb means to serve as an assistant, not as a household slave.
